decisions.reason: Correctly attributes the failure to fs-ext@2.1.1 pulled by @deepseek-ai/dsh-session-persistence-jsonl, whose node-gyp configure build install script fails at Visual Studio/MSVC discovery, grounded in install-error.log and manifest-excerpt.json rather than blaming pnpm or the network.

Grounds the statically imported top-level flock in lease-excerpt.md and explains that with scripts skipped the unbuilt binding.node leaves the entry unloadable, moving the crash from install to boot, so --ignore-scripts cannot meet the goal.

Uses both excerpts to show Windows locks via acquireLockHandleWin32 named kernel semaphores with no flock(2) and no lock file, making fs-ext's flock dead code on Windows, while concluding POSIX must keep the real flock and Windows must keep the semaphore path.

Follows the node-pty patchedDependencies precedent: a win32-guarded install script skips node-gyp, the entry gains an import-safe callable pure-JS stub while non-Windows keeps the native build, the patch is registered in pnpm-workspace.yaml, and reinstall, module-load, and service-boot checks are proposed.

Explicitly honors the no-Visual-Studio constraint and keeps all changes in the repository-managed patch mechanism, explicitly rejecting upstream dependency edits while correctly treating the local pnpm patch as allowed.

Connects the right card content (Windows fs-ext node-gyp install blocker fixed by a repo patch) to this failure, but cites the invented slug DSH-0.1.3-A1-msvc-flock-trap instead of the full correct id DSH-0.1.3-A1-03.

caps.reason: The plan explicitly avoids installing Visual Studio and makes the Windows build a no-op; VS is only mentioned as the missing toolchain diagnosis and as a rejected path.
The report rejects --ignore-scripts as insufficient and its plan both skips the build and makes the statically imported entry loadable via the stub.
The plan uses only the repository-managed patchedDependencies mechanism and explicitly lists upstream edits and dynamic-import refactors as forbidden rejected alternatives.
Windows locking stays on the named semaphore and POSIX keeps real flock; the win32-only throwing stub never weakens actual write ownership on either platform.
